adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Creating a client with a loader exposing only the fallback permanently caches it in shared CryptoIntegration, so later initialization with a full-provider loader is ignored and unsupported crypto operations fail.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows CryptoIntegration.init() is called in AuthzClient.create() at line 95 with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(). Looking at CryptoIntegration.java, the init() method uses a 'cryptoProvider' static field that once set, is never changed (detectProvider is only called if cryptoProvider is null). The AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() returning 100, while other providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return 200. If AuthzClient.create() is called first with a classloader that only has the fallback AuthzClientCryptoProvider, it will be cached permanently. Later calls with a full-provider classloader will be ignored since cryptoProvider is already set. The AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException for most operations, so this could cause failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Adding abstract order() to the public SPI breaks existing external implementations at source and runtime, so it should be a default method or separate optional priority contract.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that `int order()` is added as a new abstract method to the `CryptoProvider` interface (line 44 in CryptoProvider.java). This is a public SPI interface, and adding an abstract method without a default implementation will break binary compatibility with any existing external implementations of this interface - they will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError and won't compile without implementing the new method. The finding correctly identifies this as a breaking change that should use a default method instead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:58 — Implementing the system-wide CryptoProvider for an ECDSA-only client leaves most contract methods throwing, so unrelated future crypto calls can fail and every SPI expansion couples back to this client.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods (getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getKeyPairGen, getKeyFactory, getCertStore, etc.). This is a legitimate architectural concern - the class is registered as a system-wide CryptoProvider via META-INF/services, but only implements ECDSA-related functionality. While the order() method returns 100 (lower than the 200 returned by other providers like DefaultCryptoProvider), meaning it should be deprioritized, if it's the only provider on the classpath, calls to unimplemented methods will fail. This is a valid scope/architecture concern grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal provider priorities now silently depend on ServiceLoader iteration order, making selection nondeterministic and forcing providers to coordinate magic numbers globally.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when multiple CryptoProviders have the same order() value, the selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration order, which is not guaranteed to be deterministic. The diff shows providers are sorted by order() in reversed order (line 57), and the first one is selected. The new AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order=100, while existing providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) have order=200. While the current implementation works because orders differ, the finding raises a valid architectural concern about the design - equal priorities would lead to nondeterministic behavior. However, this is a design/architecture concern rather than a bug since the current implementation has distinct order values.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal priority for FIPS and non-FIPS providers makes mixed classpaths silently select by discovery order instead of rejecting ambiguity, potentially bypassing FIPS cryptographic enforcement.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims equal priority for FIPS and non-FIPS providers, but the diff clearly shows: DefaultCryptoProvider.order() returns 200, WildFlyElytronProvider.order() returns 200, FIPS1402Provider.order() returns 200, and AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() returns 100. The main crypto providers (FIPS, default, elytron) all have order 200, which is intentional - they are alternatives, not meant to coexist. The AuthzClientCryptoProvider has lower priority (100) so it will be ignored when a proper crypto provider is present. The code sorts by order descending and picks the highest, which is correct behavior. The finding misreads the design intent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The round-trip assertion only proves the two new converters agree with each other and never verifies the rebuilt DER signature with JCA, so symmetric encoding defects can ship unnoticed.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only verifies round-trip consistency (asn1derToConcatenatedRS -> concatenatedRSToASN1DER -> asn1derToConcatenatedRS produces the same result), but never verifies that the rebuilt DER signature can actually be verified by JCA's Signature.verify(). The test creates a signature, converts it, but the assertion at line 56 only checks that rsConcat equals rsConcat2. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added crypto conversion logic - if both converters have symmetric bugs, the test would pass but the signatures wouldn't work in practice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:56 — The new multi-provider priority selection has no test covering differing or tied orders, so a classpath-dependent provider regression could silently select an incompatible crypto implementation.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new priority-based provider selection mechanism in CryptoIntegration.java (line 56-57) that sorts providers by order() and selects the highest. While there is a test file added (ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java), it only tests ECDSA algorithm functionality, not the provider selection logic itself. The finding correctly identifies that there's no test covering the new multi-provider priority selection behavior, including edge cases like tied orders or ensuring the correct provider is selected when multiple are present. This is a legitimate concern for newly added nontrivial logic that could cause silent regressions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:125 — No test exercises malformed DER inputs such as truncated lengths, non-integer members, or wrong sequence arity, leaving the new untrusted-signature error handling unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new ASN1Decoder and ASN1Encoder classes with error handling for malformed inputs (IOException for invalid tags, truncated lengths, wrong sequence sizes, etc.). The test file ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java only tests the happy path - converting valid signatures back and forth. It does not test malformed DER inputs like truncated lengths, non-integer members, or wrong sequence arity. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for newly added error handling code paths in security-sensitive cryptographic parsing code.
